subject: Monica, mother of Augustine of Hippo
note: One writer, research and page together (SAINT-BRIEF.md). Her record is almost all Augustine's. The Confessions are quoted from J. G. Pilkington's translation (NPNF series 1, vol. 1), read in people/augustine-of-hippo/ccel-npnf101.txt; his Cassiciacum dialogues have no public-domain English we could find, so their lines are our own translations of the Latin (augustinus.it), marked on the page and as kind 'own' in monica.quotes.json. Every quotation on the page is in monica.quotes.json and verify-quotes.mjs exits 0.

life.text: Brought up in a Christian house; an old maidservant who had carried her father as a baby trained the daughters, and would not let them drink even water between meals.

As a girl sent to draw wine she began to sip, until she drank off her little cup nearly full; a maid called her 'wine-bibber' (Latin meribibula) and she renounced the habit at once. She told Augustine the story herself.
life.source: Confessions 9.8.18; Latin text, Latin Library, conf9

life.text: Married to Patricius, a pagan, 'as he was earnest in friendship, so was he violent in anger'; she never resisted him in anger; she bore 'the wronging of her bed'; her advice to bruised wives; won over her mother-in-law, who had the gossiping servants punished.
Patricius a 'poor freeman of Thagaste' (a citizen of small means).

In his sixteenth year Augustine was home from school; Patricius told Monica joyfully what he saw at the baths; she warned Augustine against fornication and adultery; he thought them 'womanish counsels'. She did not seek him a wife then, 'afraid lest a wife should prove a hindrance and a clog to my hopes' (of learning).
Patricius was won to the faith towards the end of his life; he died two years before Augustine's nineteenth year (so about 370/371); she married no one before or after him.

Augustine as a boy, near death with stomach pains, begged baptism; she would have arranged it; on his recovery it was deferred; he writes that she 'preferred that the unformed clay should be exposed to them rather than the image itself', and asks 'to what end my baptism was then deferred'.

Other accounts of the deferred baptism: Patricius agreed, 'but on the boy's recovery withdrew his consent' (Catholic Encyclopedia); her husband 'insisted that nothing be done until they were adults and could decide for themselves' (Episcopal Church).
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1911, St. Monica; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 4 May

life.text: Augustine a Manichee: she avoided having him at her table; the dream of the wooden rule and the bright youth; 'that where she was, there was I also'; her reply to his twisting of it; 'nearly nine years' more of weeping.

An unnamed bishop, reared in the Church, himself given to the Manichees as a boy, refused to argue with Augustine; 'a little vexed at her importunity' he said 'it is not possible that the son of these tears should perish'; she took it as a voice from heaven.

Carthage, 383 (the year from the live Augustine page): she held him at the shore; he lied that he was seeing a friend off; she spent the night praying in the oratory of Cyprian near the ship; he sailed; she was there next morning 'wild with grief'.
She went to church twice a day, morning and evening, not missing a day.

She followed him 'over sea and land'; comforted the sailors in a storm, assured by a vision; in Milan, told he was no longer a Manichee, she said calmly she would see him a Catholic before she died; she hung on Ambrose's words and 'loved that man as an angel of God'.

In Milan the doorkeeper stopped her bringing cakes, bread and wine to the martyrs' shrines; she gave the custom up at once at Ambrose's word; she never took more than one little cup, watered; Ambrose often praised her to Augustine.

Ambrose's answer on fasting on Saturdays (Thagaste fasted, Milan did not): 'When I am here I do not fast on Saturday; but when I am at Rome I do...'. The NPNF note says this 'has perhaps given origin to the proverb' When at Rome, do as Rome does.
life.source: Augustine, Letter 36 to Casulanus, section 32; NPNF note 441 on Confessions 6.2

life.text: She worked for a marriage for him, hoping baptism would follow; they prayed daily for a vision about it, but she saw only 'vain and fantastic things', and said she could tell God's revelations from her own dreams; the girl wanted two years of marriageable age.

The woman Augustine lived with was 'torn from my side as an impediment to my marriage', went back to Africa vowing never to know another man, and left their son; he took another mistress. Augustine does not say who sent her away (the passive voice is noted by O'Donnell).
life.source: Confessions 6.15.25; O'Donnell, commentary on 6.15.25 and on Book 6 generally

life.text: Critics and holders on the dismissal: O'Donnell, 'his wife in all but name, and his situation was not especially irregular'; 'the hard-heartedness for which moderns reproach him as with one voice'; Peter Brown (1983), quoted there: 'under the glacial weight of the late Roman caste system'. Episcopal Church: Monica 'was not without worldly ambitions and tastes' until her ambition was transformed.
life.source: O'Donnell, Augustine: Confessions (1992), commentary on 6.15.25; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022

life.text: On her advice to wives: OrthoChristian calls her 'a model of wifely forbearance' who 'tamed her husband's violent temper by her meekness'; the Episcopal Church says 'Patricius could be violent and abusive'; the Catholic blog The True Dignity of Women (27 August 2014): 'Her coping mechanism is the last thing anyone would suggest today' and 'She should not be set as an example of how to respond', while still counting her a patron for victims.

About a year before Augustine's baptism, Justina persecuted Ambrose; the people kept guard in the church; 'There my mother... lived in prayer'; hymns and psalms began to be sung in the Eastern manner.
The garden (late summer 386, the date the live Augustine page uses): Augustine and Alypius told her; 'she leapeth for joy'; he stood 'in that rule of faith' she had seen in her vision.

Cassiciacum: Verecundus lent his country house; with Alypius; 'in woman's garb truly, but with a man's faith'. On the Happy Life was held on Augustine's birthday (the Ides of November) in the baths; guests named: his mother first ('cuius meriti credo esse omne quod vivo'), Navigius, Trygetius, Licentius, cousins Lastidianus and Rusticus, Adeodatus.

Her words at Cassiciacum: the soul fed by understanding (2.8); good things wanted and had (2.10) and Augustine's 'arcem philosophiae tenuisti'; 'caducarii' for the Academics, then she rose to leave and all left laughing (2.16); Navigius's praise of the word (3.20); 'Aliud est Deum habere, aliud non esse sine Deo' (3.21); she recognised 'Fove precantes, Trinitas' from Ambrose's hymn Deus Creator omnium and closed with the happy life as the perfect life (4.35).

On Order: she scolded Licentius for singing Psalm 80:7 (Vulgate 79:8) outside while answering nature, and his joke (1.8.22); her question whether women were ever brought into such debates, and Augustine's answer and his praise of her philosophy and fearlessness of death (1.11.31-32); 'cuius ingenium quotidie mihi novum est' (2.17.45).
After the baptism she cared for the whole household 'as if she had been mother of us all; served us as if she had been child of all'.

Ostia: the talk at the window; her words 'what do I here?'; five days later a fever; she fainted, asked 'Where was I?', said 'Here shall you bury your mother'; Navigius wished she might die at home; 'Lay this body anywhere...'; she had once prepared a grave by Patricius; 'Nothing is far to God...'; she died on the ninth day of her sickness, in her fifty-sixth year, Augustine in his thirty-third.

After her death: Augustine closed her eyes; Adeodatus wailed; Evodius sang the psalm 'I will sing of mercy and judgment' (Ps 101); Augustine held back tears, bathed, slept, woke with Ambrose's hymn Deus Creator omnium, and wept 'for her and for me'.
Augustine names her only once in the Confessions, at 9.13.37 (Latin 'Monnicae'); checked by search of the Pilkington text and confirmed by O'Donnell's note on 9.9.19 ('who is named only there').

Augustine's sister: 'a widow who had long served God and lived in charge of His handmaidens'; not named by Possidius. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the daughter Perpetua and names the three children Augustine, Navigius, Perpetua.

Burial and later history: buried at Ostia, 'at first seems to have been almost forgotten'; body moved in the 500s to a hidden crypt in the church of St Aurea; cult spread about the 1200s with a feast on 4 May; 1430 Martin V had the relics brought to Rome, 'Many miracles occurred on the way'; later placed in a chapel of Sant'Agostino. A letter to 'his sister Perpetua' on her death is 'undoubtedly spurious'. 1850 Paris association of Christian mothers under her patronage, archconfraternity 1856, branches Dublin, London, Liverpool, Sydney, Buenos Aires.

Epitaph by Anicius Bassus, 'a later consul', known from manuscripts; found near Sant'Aurea at Ostia in 1945; now inside the church; Latin text of the first lines; relics taken to Sant'Agostino in Campo Marzio in 1430 by Martin V.
The 1945 find: two boys digging a hole for a goalpost in the churchyard at Ostia hit the stone.
life.source: Treasures of the Ancient Church (Substack), 27 August 2026, free part of the post

life.text: OCA: born c. 330-333 at Tagaste of Christian parents; patron in the West of 'wives and mothers whose husbands or sons have gone astray'; feast 4 May.

Santa Monica, California: the Conservancy's story (Crespí's diary, the water 'reminded him of Saint Monica's tears', 'as that day was Saint Monica's name day'); the city named after the saint. Costansó's diary dates the expedition's passage through the Los Angeles basin to 1 to 9 August 1769 (Porciúncula river forded 3 August). Her feast was then 4 May (Roman calendar, about 1550 to 1969).
life.source: Santa Monica Conservancy; Costansó, Diary (Teggart ed., 1911); Calendarium Romanum 1969

feasts.who: Roman Martyrology 1916 ('At Ostia, the birthday of St. Monica...'); Roman calendar c. 1550-1969
Roman Martyrology 1916: translation of her body from Ostia to Rome under Martin V, buried in the church of St Augustine

Catholic memorial (USCCB 2026: 'Saint Monica, Memorial'); Calendarium Romanum 1969 explains: the Augustinian hermits kept Augustine's conversion on 5 May in the 1400s and chose 4 May for Monica, 'cuius dies natalis ignoratur'; in the Roman calendar about 1550; moved in 1969
Church of England, 'Monica, mother of Augustine of Hippo, 387' (set as a Lesser Festival in the printed calendar's layout)
LCMS (Lutheran Service Book): 'Monica, Mother of Augustine'
Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: 'Monica, Mother of Augustine of Hippo, 387'
ELCA, Evangelical Lutheran Worship: 'Monica, mother of Augustine, 387'

could_not_verify: Her birthplace: only later writers (Catholic Encyclopedia, OCA, saint.gr) say Thagaste; the page says 'most likely'.
That she was of Berber descent (Episcopal Church, OrthoChristian): no early source; left off the page.
The name Perpetua for Augustine's sister: only later writers; the page says so.

Which spring the Portolá expedition named on 3 August 1769 (Costansó: Ojo de Agua de los Alisos), and whether it is the one later called the Tears of Santa Monica: not settled from sources on disk; the page does not identify them and says only that the expedition passed in August, when her feast was 4 May.
Crespí's own diary was not fetched (Bolton's 1927 edition); the Conservancy's report of it is quoted as the Conservancy's.
No public-domain English translation of On the Happy Life or On Order was found; the page's English for them is ours, marked beside each line.
The exact day and month of her death: unknown (Calendarium Romanum 1969: 'cuius dies natalis ignoratur').
The Frick panel's identification as Monica is the museum's (in brackets).

checked: Every number and date against the texts on disk: her age 55 and his 32 (Confessions 9.11), 'nearly nine years' (3.11), twice a day (5.9), one naming (9.13.37, O'Donnell), the sixteenth year (2.3), Patricius dead two years before his nineteenth (3.4), 383, 385 to 387, 13 November 386 (On the Happy Life 1.6, Latin), 1430, 1945, 1850 and 1856 (Catholic Encyclopedia, ostia-antica.org, Treasures of the Ancient Church).

Every feast in its calendar text: the Calendarium Romanum 1969 commentary (the 1400s Augustinian choice of 4 May, the Roman calendar about 1550, the move to 27 August), the 1916 Martyrology (9 April, 4 May), USCCB, CofE, LFF, LSB, ELCA, OCA, saint.gr, OrthoChristian's 'May 4/17'.

Attributions and the Latin: each 'our translation' line read in the Latin on disk (caducarii and Navigius's 'male latino, sed aptissimo'; the women-in-philosophy question and 'philosophia tua mihi plurimum placet'; Licentius and the psalm; 'Aliud est, inquit mater, Deum habere'; 'nulla re alia credo'; her closing line after 'Fove precantes, Trinitas'); 'nihil longe est deo' and 'meribibulam' in the Latin of Confessions 9; 'did we daily beg of Thee' in 6.13 (so 'Mother and son prayed' is right); the LFF, OrthoChristian, True Dignity of Women, O'Donnell and Catholic Encyclopedia lines in context; the Santa Monica story against the Conservancy text and Costanso's diary.

Rules: capitals for God, italics, plain sentences, number tiles, seo lengths (title 62, description 154). Licences read on the Commons file pages through the API (Tristan and Piero both public domain). Band and portrait looked at downscaled; the card is the test's face.

changed: Her name: cut 'Where the name comes from is not known.' No text on disk says so, and a Berber or Punic origin is often proposed.
Her closing line at Cassiciacum was 'The last word of the birthday dialogue'; Augustine speaks after her to close it (On the Happy Life 4.36). Now 'Her last word in the birthday dialogue.'
for_owner: Number tile 'Times her son names her: 1'. It is true and striking, and the lines explain it ('my mother', 'Thy handmaid'), but after the rejected 'Signs he performed: 0' you may read it as a slight on Augustine. Kept.
The Santa Monica myth rests on the August 1769 dates in Costanso's diary and her 4 May feast. The 1770 journeys are not discussed; no text on disk covers them.
The writer's picture notes stand: Piero's Frick panel is cracked and named 'An Augustinian Nun (Saint Monica)' by the Frick; the band is 694 KB.
